name: int() used on text with a decimal point
description: Casts input such as "3.5" with int(), expecting it to become 3 or 3.5. int() only accepts text that is a whole number, so Python stops with a ValueError. float() is needed for real numbers.
explanation: It looks like int() was given text with a decimal point in it, which int() can't cast. int() only works on whole numbers like "42". Think about what kind of number the user types here, and which casting function fits it.

name: bool() expected to read the word True or False
description: Uses bool(input()) or bool(text) expecting "False" or "no" to become False. bool() of any non-empty text is True, so every answer counts as True. Comparing the text, for example answer == "yes", is needed.
explanation: It looks like bool() was used to turn typed text into True or False. bool() only checks whether the text is empty, so any word at all, even False or no, gives True. Think about how to test what the user actually typed instead.

name: = instead of == (or the other way round)
description: Uses a single = (which stores a value) where == (which compares two values) is needed, for example in an if condition, or uses == where a value should be stored.
explanation: It looks like = and == have been mixed up. A single = stores a value in a variable, and == asks whether two values are the same. Look at each = in your code and ask: is this line storing a value, or comparing two?

name: Separate ifs instead of elif
description: Writes a chain of separate if statements where only one branch should run, so more than one message can be printed. Or expects separate if statements to behave like elif.
explanation: More than one branch may be running when only one should. Separate if statements are each checked, one after another, but in an if/elif chain Python stops at the first condition that is True. Try the input yourself and count how many messages your code prints.

name: < instead of <= (or the other way round)
description: Gets the boundary value wrong with 'less than': uses < where <= is needed, or <= where < is needed, so the program is wrong for the value exactly on the boundary.
explanation: Your program seems to go wrong for the value exactly on the boundary. < means 'less than' and leaves the boundary value out, while <= means 'less than or equal to' and includes it. Read the task again to decide whether the boundary value itself should count, then test it.

name: > instead of >= (or the other way round)
description: Gets the boundary value wrong with 'greater than': uses > where >= is needed, or >= where > is needed, so the program is wrong for the value exactly on the boundary.
explanation: Your program seems to go wrong for the value exactly on the boundary. > means 'greater than' and leaves the boundary value out, while >= means 'greater than or equal to' and includes it. Read the task again to decide whether the boundary value itself should count, then test it.

name: Missing else
description: Leaves out the else branch, so nothing is printed when the if condition is False.
explanation: Nothing seems to be printed when the condition is False. An if on its own only does something when its condition is True. Check what the task wants to happen otherwise, and whether your code has a branch for it.

name: Input not turned into a number
description: Forgets that input() always gives text, so doesn't use int() before doing maths or comparing with a number. This causes an error, or text being repeated or joined instead of added.
explanation: It looks like a value from input() is being used as text, not as a number. input() always gives you text, even if the user types digits, so maths and comparisons don't work as expected. Check where you read the input and whether it is turned into a number before you use it.

name: Order of operations (BIDMAS)
description: Expects Python to work left to right, or leaves out brackets that are needed, for example writing a + b / 2 for the mean of a and b.
explanation: Python may be working out your sum in a different order from the one you meant. It follows BIDMAS: brackets first, then powers, then * and /, then + and -. Work through your expression one step at a time, the way Python does, and see whether you need brackets.

name: // mixed up with /
description: Uses / (which always gives a decimal answer) where // (whole-number division) is needed, or expects / to give a whole number.
explanation: The two kinds of division may have been mixed up. / always gives a decimal answer (7 / 2 is 3.5), while // gives only the whole-number part. Check which kind of answer the task asks for.

name: Joining text and a number with +
description: Uses + to join text and a number without str(), which causes an error. A comma in print() or str() around the number is needed.
explanation: It looks like text and a number are being joined with +. Python can add two numbers, or join two pieces of text, but it can't do both at once. Find the line that joins text and a number, and think about how to make both parts the same type, or use a comma in print().

name: Loop variable never changes
description: The value tested in a while loop's condition is never changed inside the loop (for example a counter isn't increased or the next input isn't read), so the loop never ends or runs out of input.
explanation: Your loop seems to keep going for ever. A while loop only stops when its condition becomes False, so something inside the loop must change the value the condition checks. Find the variable in your loop's condition and check where the loop changes it.

name: if used where a loop is needed
description: Uses if where while is needed, so the check only happens once instead of repeating until the condition is False.
explanation: Your check only seems to happen once. An if checks its condition one time, but a while loop keeps checking and repeating until the condition is False. Ask yourself whether this part of the program needs to repeat.

name: Loop that never runs
description: Sets up a while loop whose condition is already False at the start (for example the wrong comparison, or a starting value that stops it), or a for loop over an empty range (for example counting down with a positive step), so the loop body runs zero times.
explanation: Your loop doesn't seem to run at all. If a while condition is already False at the start, or a range is empty, Python skips the loop body completely. Check the starting value and the condition (or the range's start, stop and step) using the first value your program gets.

name: Thinks range includes the stop value
description: Thinks range(1, 5) includes 5, so expects one number too many, or writes a stop value one too small and the loop runs one time too few.
explanation: Your loop seems to run one time too many or too few. range stops just before its stop value, so range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3 and 4 but not 5. List the numbers your range gives and compare them with what the task needs.

name: Wrong start for range(n)
description: Thinks range(5) starts at 5 or at 1, instead of 0 (it gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 4). So expects the numbers 1 to 5, or uses range(n) where the loop variable must start at 1.
explanation: Your loop seems to start at the wrong number. range(n) with one number starts at 0, not at 1 or at n. Write out the first few values your loop variable takes and check them against the task.

name: Changing the loop variable inside a for loop
description: Changes the loop variable inside a for loop (for example i = i + 1) and expects that to change the loop. In Python, the for loop gives the variable its next value from the range each time round, so the change only affects the rest of that time round.
explanation: The loop variable seems to be changed inside a for loop. A for loop gives the variable its next value from the range each time round, so changing it inside the loop doesn't change how many times the loop runs. Think about whether to change the range instead, or to use a separate variable.

name: Inner loop runs the wrong number of times
description: In nested loops, the inner loop runs the wrong number of times (for example range(row) instead of range(4), so each row is a different length), or the outer loop's variable is reset inside the inner loop.
explanation: The inner loop seems to run the wrong number of times. With nested loops, the whole inner loop runs once for every time round the outer loop. Check what the inner loop's range uses, and that the outer loop's variable isn't changed inside it.

name: Counting positions from 1
description: Treats the first character of a string or the first item of a list as index 1, so it uses [1] for the first, [len()] for the last, or adds 1 to what find() gives. Indexing in Python counts from 0.
explanation: It looks like the positions were counted from 1. In Python, indexing counts from 0, so the first character or item is [0] and the last is [len() - 1]. Check each index you used against that.

name: Thinks a slice includes its end index
description: Writes text[0:4] to get 3 characters, or expects text[0:3] to include the character at index 3. A slice stops just BEFORE its end index, like range().
explanation: It looks like the slice was expected to include its end index. A slice such as text[0:3] stops just before index 3, so it gives the characters at 0, 1 and 2. Count how many characters you want, then check where the slice stops.

name: Thinks upper(), lower() or replace() change the string
description: Calls a string method such as text.upper() or text.replace(...) on its own line and expects text to change. Strings can't be changed: the method gives back a new string, which must be stored, for example text = text.upper().
explanation: It looks like a string method was expected to change the variable by itself. upper(), lower() and replace() give back a NEW string and leave the old one as it was. Store the result, for example text = text.replace("a", "b").

name: Thinks randint() leaves out the top number
description: Writes random.randint(1, 7) for a dice, or randint(low, high - 1), as if randint worked like range(). random.randint(a, b) can give a, b or any whole number between.
explanation: It looks like randint() was treated like range(), which stops before its end. random.randint(1, 6) can give 6, so a dice is randint(1, 6). Check the lowest and highest numbers you want, and use exactly those.

name: Thinks a stored random number changes each time it is used
description: Picks a random number once and stores it (often before a loop), then uses that variable as if it gave a new random number each time. A variable keeps the same value until it is assigned again, so randint() must run again for each new roll.
explanation: It looks like a stored random number was expected to change by itself. randint() picks a number when that line runs, and the variable keeps it. To get a new number each time, call randint() again, for example inside the loop.

name: Stores what append() gives back
description: Writes items = items.append(x), expecting the new list back. append() changes the list itself and gives back None, so the list is lost and items becomes None.
explanation: It looks like the result of append() was stored back in the list's variable. append() changes the list itself and gives back None, so the variable now holds None. Write items.append(x) on its own.

name: Defines a function but never calls it
description: Writes the function with def but never calls it (or writes its name without brackets), so its lines never run and nothing is printed. def only makes the function; a call such as greet() runs it.
explanation: It looks like the function was defined but never called. def only makes the function: its lines run when you call it, with its name and brackets, such as menu(). Check that your program calls each function it needs.

name: Puts quotes round a variable passed to a function
description: Calls a function with "name" instead of name, so the word itself is passed, not the variable's value (or doesn't notice the quotes when reading a call).
explanation: It looks like a variable was passed with quotes round it. Quotes make it text, so the function gets the word itself, not what the variable holds. Pass the variable without quotes.

name: Forgets return, so the function gives back None
description: Works out a value inside the function but has no return line, so the call gives back None, and printing the result shows None.
explanation: It looks like the function works out its answer but never returns it. A function with no return line gives back None, which is what gets printed or stored. Add a return line with the value.

name: Prints the answer instead of returning it
description: Uses print() inside the function instead of return, so the value is shown but the call gives back None to whatever stores or prints the result.
explanation: It looks like the function prints its answer instead of returning it. print() only shows the value; the call still gives back None. Use return so the result can be stored and used.

name: Calls a function but doesn't store its result
description: Calls a function that returns a value, such as bonus(score), on its own line, and expects a variable to change. The returned value is lost unless it is stored, for example score = bonus(score).
explanation: It looks like the function's result was expected to change a variable by itself. A returned value is lost unless you store it, for example score = bonus(score). Check where each result goes.

name: Uses mode "w" to add to a file
description: Opens a file with mode "w" to add more to it, but "w" starts the file again, empty. Mode "a" adds to the end.
explanation: It looks like mode "w" was used to add to a file. "w" empties the file each time it is opened, so what was there before is lost. Use mode "a" to add to the end.

name: Thinks write() starts a new line
description: Writes several values with write() and expects each on its own line, but write() adds no new line, so they run together. + "\n" is needed.
explanation: It looks like write() was expected to start a new line by itself. write() writes exactly the text it is given, so the values run together on one line. Add + "\n" to end each line.

name: Forgets that each line read keeps its \n
description: Reads lines from a file and uses them without strip(), so each line still ends in \n: printing gives blank lines between, and comparing with a word never matches.
explanation: It looks like each line was used as if it had no \n on the end. A line read from a file keeps its new line, so it prints a blank line after it and never equals a plain word. Use line.strip() first.

name: Puts the column before the row
description: Uses grid[col][row] instead of grid[row][col], or goes down the columns when reading row by row, so the wrong item is used.
explanation: It looks like the row and column were swapped. In grid[row][col] the first index picks the row (the inner list) and the second picks the item in it. Check which index is the row.

name: Mixes up len(grid) and len(grid[0])
description: Uses len(grid) for the number of columns or len(grid[0]) for the number of rows, which only works when the grid is square.
explanation: It looks like the number of rows and columns were mixed up. len(grid) counts the rows, and len(grid[0]) counts the items in one row, which is the number of columns. Check each len() against what you need.

name: Uses and where or is needed, or the reverse
description: Joins two parts of a check with the wrong word: and when either part should be enough (a value below the lowest or above the highest), or or when both must be true (a length of at least 3 and at most 10). The check then lets everything through, or nothing.
explanation: It looks like and and or were swapped. and needs both parts to be True, but or needs only one of them. Ask yourself whether both rules must hold at once, or whether breaking either one is enough.

name: A while loop whose condition never changes
description: Asks again inside the loop but stores the new answer in a different variable, so the variable in the loop's condition never changes and the loop never ends (it keeps asking until there is no more input).
explanation: It looks like your loop asks again but never changes what the condition checks. The new answer has to go back into the same variable that the while condition uses. Otherwise the condition stays the same and the loop never stops.

name: Expects .isdigit() to accept negative numbers or decimals
description: Uses .isdigit() alone as a type check where negative numbers (or decimals) are allowed. .isdigit() is False for "-3" and "2.5" because - and . are not digits, so valid answers are refused.
explanation: It looks like your type check refuses negative numbers. .isdigit() is only True when every character is a digit, and - is not a digit. If negative numbers are allowed, also accept a - followed by digits.

name: Uses == to compare with a list of allowed values
description: Writes answer == ["yes", "no"] instead of answer in ["yes", "no"]. A single string is never equal to a whole list, so every answer is refused.
explanation: It looks like the answer is being compared with the whole list. == checks whether two things are the same, and one word is never the same as a list. Use in to check whether the answer is one of the items in the list.

name: Casts with int() before checking for an empty answer
description: Converts the input with int() before the presence check. int("") stops the program with a ValueError, so the check for an empty answer is never reached.
explanation: It looks like int() runs before the check for an empty answer. int("") stops the program with an error, so your presence check never gets a chance. Check the answer while it is still text, and cast it with int() afterwards.

name: Compares usernames without allowing for capital letters
description: Compares the typed username with the stored one using == alone when usernames should ignore capitals, so Ben_K is refused for ben_k. (Passwords are still compared exactly.)
explanation: It looks like the username check is treating capital letters as different. Here usernames should match whatever capitals are used, so compare username.lower() with the stored username. Passwords are different: they must match exactly.

name: The failed-attempt counter is never increased
description: Writes failed + 1 (which works out a number and throws it away), or leaves the increase out, so the counter of attempts stays at 0: the count is wrong, or a limit of three attempts never ends the loop.
explanation: It looks like the counter of attempts never goes up. failed + 1 works out a new number but doesn't store it anywhere. Store the new number back in the same variable, so the counter really changes each time.

name: Gives no result when the item isn't in the list
description: The linear search only prints (or returns) something when the item is found. When the item isn't in the list the program prints nothing, or returns None, instead of saying it wasn't found.
explanation: It looks like your search only says something when it finds the item. When the item isn't in the list, the loop ends and nothing tells the user. Add the "not found" result after the loop, so it is given once every item has been checked.

name: The search stops before the last item
description: The loop of a linear search ends one item too soon, usually range(len(items) - 1) or while i < len(items) - 1, so the last item is never checked and an item at the end is reported as not found.
explanation: It looks like your loop stops before it reaches the last item. range(len(items)) already stops at the last index, len(items) - 1, so taking 1 away misses that item. Check the loop goes all the way to the end of the list.

name: Uses binary search on a list that isn't sorted
description: Runs a binary search (or expects it to work) on a list that isn't in order. Throwing away half the list only works when every item in that half is known to be too small or too big, so the search can miss an item that is there.
explanation: It looks like you expected binary search to work on a list that isn't in order. Binary search throws away half the list because it knows every item there is too small or too big, which is only true in a sorted list. Check the list is sorted first, or use a linear search.

name: low or high never changes in a binary search
description: After checking the middle item, low or high is not moved past it (for example low = mid instead of low = mid + 1, or one of them is never changed), so the part of the list left to search stops getting smaller and the loop never ends or checks the wrong part.
explanation: It looks like the part of the list left to search never gets smaller. After checking the middle item, move past it: set low to one after mid if the item you want is bigger, or high to one before mid if it is smaller. Otherwise low and high stay the same and the loop goes on for ever.

name: Finds the middle with / instead of //
description: Works out the middle index as (low + high) / 2, which gives a real number such as 2.5 (or 2.0). A list index must be a whole number, so the program stops with a TypeError, or prints the decimal index.
explanation: It looks like you found the middle with /, which always gives a real number such as 3.5. A list index must be a whole number, so add low and high, then divide with //, which drops the remainder. Then mid is always a whole number you can use for indexing.

name: A bubble sort pass checks one pair too many or too few
description: The inner loop of a bubble sort goes one step too far (range(len(items)), so items[j + 1] is past the end) or stops one pair early (range(len(items) - 2)), so the last pair is never compared.
explanation: It looks like your pass compares one pair too many or too few. A list of n items has n - 1 pairs next to each other, so j goes from 0 to n - 2 with range(len(items) - 1). Then items[j + 1] is always in the list, and the last pair is still checked.

name: Swaps two values without a temporary variable
description: Swaps with items[j] = items[j + 1] then items[j + 1] = items[j]. The first line overwrites items[j], so both places end up holding the same value and one value is lost.
explanation: It looks like one of the two values was lost in the swap. Once the first place is overwritten, its old value is gone, so the second line copies the same value back. Keep the first value in a temp variable before you overwrite it, or swap both values in one line, as in a, b = b, a.

name: Overwrites a value before it has been moved
description: In an insertion sort, an item is written into a place before the value already there has been moved or saved: for example the key is put in the gap before the shift, or the shift copies to the left instead of to the right, so a value is lost or repeated.
explanation: It looks like a value was written over before it was moved. In insertion sort, each bigger item is copied one place to the right first, which makes a gap. Only put the item you are inserting into the gap once the shifting has finished.

name: Doesn't keep the item being inserted
description: The item being inserted is not stored in a variable (key = items[i]) before the shift. The first shift copies the item to its left over items[i], so the program later inserts the wrong value and one value appears twice.
explanation: It looks like the item you are inserting was lost during the shift. The first shift copies the item to its left into its place, so that position no longer holds it. Keep it in a variable (key) before the shifting starts, and put key into the gap at the end.

name: A merge leaves out items from one half
description: When one half runs out, the merge stops without adding the items still left in the other half (the leftovers), so the merged list is shorter than the two halves together.
explanation: It looks like some items were left out of the merged list. The loop stops as soon as one half runs out, but the other half can still have items in it. After the loop, add whatever is left in both halves, so the merged list has every item.

name: Merges without comparing the front items
description: Joins the two halves end to end (left + right), or takes items from them in turn, without comparing the front item of each half, so the merged list isn't in order.
explanation: It looks like the halves were joined without comparing them. Merging only gives a sorted list if each step compares the front item of each half and takes the smaller one. Then move along in the half you took from, and compare again.
